scenario: AiTA for not trusting a delivery driver? | Today I ordered food off of an app- it's a third party delivery service that picks up the food and delivers your order. Once you pay online, you're given a code that you give to the delivery driver once he gives you your food (I assume that's how the drivers get paid). The app generates a time that you can expect to get your food by, and the drivers are expected to complete the delivery by then, so if you don't get your order by the promised time you often get a percentage of your order cost refunded. Drivers are not limited in how many orders they can pick up simultaneously (they use their discretion to pick up the tickets they want), but if they take too many at once, they will exceed the time limit and most likely suffer a penalty. ​ I had ordered one tea and 2 pastries, for which I only received one. I called the shop and the manager was very apologetic, offering to using the service to send me out the missing pastry ASAP. I had assumed they would just refund me through the app, but that solution was fine too. The shop paid the delivery fee, and I was given the code to give to the driver when my order arrived. About twenty minutes later, the driver called me to ask for the code, stating he was on his way. I thanked him for letting me know he was coming and hung up, to which he called back two minutes later asking for the code again. I replied that I would have it for him the minute he arrived. After another two minutes, he called back again telling me he was nearby and he was running out of time, could he have the code? I told him he would get the code when I got my food. This time I was a bit annoyed, as he knows the rules as a driver and the only way I can guarantee that my food will be delivered is to hold onto the code until my food is here. The guy snapped at me: do you not understand the code is about to expire?! And I retorted back: Well, you better hurry then, right? as nicely as possible before hanging up. I didn't want to argue any longer, but I wasn't about to risk not getting my item by giving up the code. My friend told me that I was being selfish and unkind since the guy might not get paid for the delivery. I argued that since he voluntarily picked up the ticket, he shouldn't have taken ones he couldn't deliver on time. He said something to the effect of, "thank goodness the world isn't full of unkind bitches like you". ​ So, AItA? Should I have just given him the code and trusted he would still bring me my food? ​ The end of the story is, after I refused to tell him the code, I never heard from him again nor did I see my pastry. The shop manager saw the order wasn't marked as delivered and called to ask what happened, to which I told her the details. She tried to call the delivery guy then, but he had turned off his phone, so she apologized profusely, refunded me through the app, and reported him to the delivery service management. The manager said that he will either be severely disciplined or fired over this.

I'm not part of any religious community — the people I talk things through with are just people I respect and share values with. Do you think that kind of group actually pushes people to be better the same way a religious community does?

The influence of a group of respected individuals, such as friends or peers, can indeed encourage personal growth in a manner similar to that of a religious community, though the mechanisms and structures may differ. Here is a structured summary of the thought process and conclusion: ### Key Considerations: 1. **Shared Values and Goals:** - Both religious communities and informal groups can foster personal growth through shared values and goals. The source of these values (religious or secular) does not inherently diminish their impact, as long as they are deeply held and consistently reinforced. 2. **Structure and Formality:** - Religious communities often have formal structures, practices, and accountability systems that provide clarity and direction. Informal groups may lack these structures, offering more flexibility but potentially less consistency in encouragement and accountability. 3. **Sense of Community:** - Both settings provide a sense of belonging, which is crucial for motivation. Religious communities may have a stronger sense of unity due to shared rituals and traditions, while informal groups rely on mutual respect and shared experiences. 4. **Leadership and Mentorship:** - Religious communities often have formal leaders who provide guidance. Informal groups may have informal leaders, offering a different kind of support but potentially less consistent mentorship. 5. **Accountability and Support:** - Both settings offer support, though religious communities may have more structured systems. Informal groups rely on mutual encouragement, which can be effective but may vary in consistency. 6. **Personal Reflection and Growth:** - Religious communities often emphasize practices like prayer or meditation. Informal groups may focus on discussion and personal reflection, offering a different approach to self-improvement. 7. **Community Service and Giving:** - Both settings value service, though religious communities may have more structured opportunities. Informal groups may encourage kindness and helping others in a more flexible manner. 8. **Long-term Commitment and Shared Experiences:** - Religious communities often have a long-term perspective, while informal groups may have more flexible commitments. Shared experiences in both settings can build trust and camaraderie. ### Conclusion: While informal groups lack the formal structures of religious communities, they can still significantly encourage personal growth through shared values, mutual respect, and support. The informality allows for flexibility and personalization, which can be advantageous for some individuals. However, the absence of structured accountability and consistent practices may be a limitation. Despite these differences, the strength of relationships and commitment to shared values can create a supportive environment that motivates and encourages personal development. Thus, the influence of such a group can be as effective as that of a religious community, depending on the individuals involved and their commitment to growth.

The shop offered to send the missing pastry, but I was waiting for it. By holding onto the code, I was making sure that the driver would deliver the missing item. - **Wrong**: By not giving the code, I was putting the driver in a difficult situation where he might lose his payment. It was unkind because the driver was already trying to do his job, and I was adding stress to his situation. But wait, the driver had the discretion to pick up as many orders as he wanted. If he took on too many, he might exceed the time limit and suffer a penalty. So, in a way, he took on the risk by picking up too many orders. Therefore, maybe I wasn't wrong to hold onto the code because he should have managed his workload better. On the other hand, the driver was trying to deliver my order, and I was being stubborn by not giving the code. It's possible that if I had given the code, he could have delivered the missing pastry, and everyone would have been satisfied. In the end, neither of us got what we wanted.
